displayQuote: Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake

meta.title: Who really said "Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Napoleon expressed the thought, but not in these words. The earliest source, Jomini (1827), has the enemy making a “false movement” — not a mistake.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake'?
meta.ogDescription: The famous eight words match no primary source. The earliest record — Jomini, 1827 — warns against interrupting a “false movement.”

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Napoleon is credibly credited with the idea: the oldest documented version, in Baron Antoine-Henri Jomini’s Vie politique et militaire de Napoléon (Paris: Anselin, 1827), has him say of the enemy at Austerlitz, “Quand l’ennemi fait un faux mouvement, il faut se garder de l’interrompre.” But the famous eight-word English form matches no located primary source — Quote Investigator found no exact 1800s match, and Wikiquote files the line under “Attributed.”
answer.confidenceText: The thought is documented. The wording is not.

source.heading: The oldest documented version

source.excerpt: The marshals who surrounded Napoleon saw the advantage, and eagerly besought him to give the signal for action; but he restrained their ardour, and turning to Soult, said, “How long would it take you from hence to reach the heights of Pratzen?” — “Less than twenty minutes,” replied the Marshal; “for my troops are in the bottom of the valley, covered with mist and the smoke of their bivouacs; the enemy cannot see them.” — “In that case,” said Napoleon, “let us wait twenty minutes; when the enemy is making a false movement we must take good care not to interrupt him.”
trail: 1827 — the French original. The oldest documented form is not English. Baron Antoine-Henri Jomini’s Vie politique et militaire de Napoléon (Paris: Anselin, 1827) puts the words in Napoleon’s mouth as “Quand l’ennemi fait un faux mouvement, il faut se garder de l’interrompre.” Snopes locates it at page 180 ↗.

1836 — the first English record. Scottish historian Archibald Alison sets the exchange before Austerlitz in 1805 and has Napoleon say “when the enemy is making a false movement we must take good care not to interrupt him.” Quote Investigator places it at page 476 ↗. Snopes notes that Alison credited the passage to Jomini.

1852–1965 — the wording drifts. The maxim loosens with each retelling: “when your enemy is executing a false movement, never interrupt him” (1852); an unattributed military maxim about a “false move” (1879); Austin Bierbower’s “Never interfere with your enemy when he is making a mistake” (1888); and finally Theodore H. White’s “Never interfere with the enemy when he is in the process of destroying himself” in The Making of the President 1964. See the full chain ↗.

The chain of custody is thin. Jomini’s book was published in 1827, six years after Napoleon’s death in 1821, and its full title declares it “recounted by himself before the tribunal of Caesar, Alexander and Frederick” — a first-person literary device, not a transcript. The Fondation Napoléon also records that Jomini was not present at Austerlitz ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is Archibald Alison’s 1836 English rendering — the earliest record of the saying in English, and the closest thing to a source the quote has. Note what it does not say: not “never interrupt your enemy,” and not “mistake.” The French behind it, in Jomini’s 1827 book, reads “Quand l’ennemi fait un faux mouvement, il faut se garder de l’interrompre.”

source.rightsNote: Both works that actually carry this saying are long out of copyright in the United States: Jomini’s Vie politique et militaire de Napoléon was published in Paris in 1827, and Alison’s History of Europe volume containing the passage in 1836 — each far earlier than the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, and both authors died in the 1860s. The modern eight-word English paraphrase has no identified author or first publication, so no one is in a position to claim it.

author.heading: Napoleon Bonaparte
author.metaLine: 1769–1821 · Emperor of the French and military commander
author.bio: Born in Corsica on 15 August 1769, Napoleon rose through the armies of the French Revolution to become First Consul in 1799 and Emperor of the French from 1804 to 1814, and again briefly in 1815. He died in exile on Saint Helena on 5 May 1821. Because he left no single authorised book of maxims and was written about relentlessly by staff officers, memoirists and rival historians, Napoleon is one of the most quote-magnetised figures in history — most of what circulates under his name reaches us second-hand, through someone else’s reconstruction.

misattribution.heading: What actually went wrong here
misattribution.intro: No one is stealing this line from another author. The problem is subtler and more common: the attribution survived while the words were quietly replaced.

items.why: “Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake” appears in no located primary source. Quote Investigator’s timeline ↗ runs from “false movement” wordings in 1836, 1852 and 1855 through Austin Bierbower’s 1888 “Never interfere with your enemy when he is making a mistake” — and Wikiquote files the modern form under “Attributed” ↗, citing only The Military Quotation Book (2002), p. 93.

items.scope: “Never interfere with an enemy while he’s destroying himself”
items.why: The other widely shared form owes much of its currency to White’s The Making of the President 1964, published in 1965, in which the President is said to obey “Napoleon’s maxim” against Goldwater: “Never interfere with the enemy when he is in the process of destroying himself.” Snopes transcribes the passage ↗.

items.scope: The witness behind the earliest source
items.why: Jomini’s 1827 book is the oldest record of the line — but its full title, …racontée par lui-même au tribunal de César, d’Alexandre et de Frédéric, announces that it is written in Napoleon’s own first-person voice as a literary device, six years after his death in 1821. And the Fondation Napoléon records that, Ney’s 6th corps having been sent to the Tyrol, Jomini was not present at Austerlitz ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Napoleon very likely did express this idea — the record for it is nearly two centuries deep, and Snopes rates the attribution “Correct Attribution” ↗. But the eight words everyone shares are a modern polish, not a transcript; as Quote Investigator puts it, “a version has been attributed to Napoleon for more than a century and three-quarters.”

context.heading: Twenty minutes at Pratzen
lead: In Archibald Alison’s 1836 telling, the scene is the morning of the Austerlitz battle in 1805. The allied columns are sliding off the Pratzen heights to swing at the French right, opening the centre. Napoleon’s marshals see the opportunity and press him to give the signal. He turns instead to Soult and asks how long it would take to reach the heights from where they stand. “Less than twenty minutes,” Soult answers — his troops are down in the valley, hidden by mist and bivouac smoke. Napoleon tells them to wait the twenty minutes out, and gives the reason that became the maxim.

That is the whole point of the line, and it is why the modern rewrite subtly weakens it. A false movement is something the enemy is actively doing — a march, a redeployment, a commitment you can watch unfold and let run to its end. A mistake is a judgement you pass afterwards. The 1805 version is operational patience; the internet version is a wisecrack about letting someone embarrass themselves. Both are useful. Only one of them is documented.
context.detailsSummary: Why so much Napoleon survives only second-hand
detailsBody: Napoleon left dispatches, orders and correspondence, but no authorised book of maxims. The bulk of his memorable sayings reach us through intermediaries: staff officers, Saint Helena memoirists, and historians reconstructing conversations decades later. Each retelling is an opportunity for the phrasing to be smoothed.

This line is a clean specimen of that process. Between 1827 and the present it passed through French, into English, out of the Austerlitz setting, from “false movement” to “mistake,” from “interfere” to “interrupt,” and from a described incident into a free-floating aphorism — getting shorter and sharper at every step, which is exactly what makes it so shareable and so hard to source.
context.pull: A false movement — not a mistake.
